standard.title: Responses to characters and events across contexts
standard.description: identify responses to characters and events in literary texts, drawn from historical, social or cultural contexts, by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify aspects of literary texts that represent details or information about historical, social and cultural experiences (AC9E5LE01). They have not yet examined how the historical, social or cultural context of a text shapes responses to its characters and events, nor read widely across First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify their own and others' responses to characters and events in literary texts from diverse historical, social and cultural contexts, and explain how context shapes those responses.

nodes.label: Context shapes response
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how the historical, social or cultural context of a text may influence how readers respond to characters, actions and events.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one way that the historical, social or cultural context of a provided text shapes how readers respond to a character or event; explain why a response might differ from a reader of a different time or context.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how historical, social and cultural experiences embedded in a text may produce different responses to characters and events; explain how a reader's own context also shapes their response.
wider: Compare responses to the same character from a contemporary reader and a reader from the historical context of the text
Examine how responses to heroes in texts from different cultural contexts (e.g. First Nations Australian texts vs. Western adventure narratives) reflect different values
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat their own response as universal cannot engage meaningfully with diverse authors in Node 2 or evaluate others' responses in Node 3 — both require the foundational understanding that response is contextually situated.

response_modes.reason: Moving from 'I respond to this character in this way' to 'I respond this way because of my context, and someone from a different context might respond differently' requires explicit scaffolding. Students often treat their response as universal without prompting to consider its situatedness.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-cultural comparison of responses to characters is genuinely rich — it develops empathy, cultural understanding, and connects to First Nations Australian literature in ways that go beyond identification toward genuine interpretive engagement.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one way that a text's context shapes a reader's response to a character or event
Explains how a reader from a different time or context might respond differently to the same character or event

nodes.label: Reading across diverse authors
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors and describe features of the literary contexts they represent.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and describe the context (historical, social, or cultural) represented in at least one text from a First Nations Australian author or a world author from a different cultural context.
nodes.typical_width: Read and respond to texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors; discuss how the contexts represented in these texts shape their characters, events and themes; share personal responses and connect them to the texts' contexts.
wider: Compare how two authors from different cultural backgrounds represent a shared theme (e.g. family, belonging, courage) and analyse what the similarities and differences reveal
Explore reviews of Australian films and identify how reviewers interpret cultural contexts in their responses

response_modes.reason: Reading across diverse authors requires accumulating a range of textual encounters — responses to diverse contexts cannot be built from analysis of a single text. The wider the reading repertoire, the more textured students' understanding of how context shapes response becomes.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Reading First Nations Australian authors and engaging critically with their contexts is both required by ACARA and genuinely rich — it builds cultural knowledge, empathy and interpretive complexity that extends far beyond a single text.
success_criteria: Names the cultural, historical or social context of at least one text by a First Nations Australian or world author
Shares a personal response to a character or event and connects it to the text's context

nodes.label: Sharing and evaluating responses
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can share and evaluate responses to characters and events in texts from diverse contexts, explaining how context shapes their own and others' readings.
nodes.minimum_width: Share a personal response to a character or event from a text by a First Nations Australian or world author and connect the response to one aspect of the text's context.
nodes.typical_width: Share and evaluate responses to texts from diverse historical, social and cultural contexts; explain how own and others' responses are shaped by context; compare responses across the class and discuss how different readers may respond differently to the same character or event.
wider: Compare personal responses to a First Nations Australian text with those of a classmate and discuss how different contexts produce different readings
Evaluate a published review of a text from a different cultural context and analyse how the reviewer's context shapes their response

response_modes.reason: Sharing and evaluating responses requires integrating understanding of how context shapes meaning (Node 1) and reading experience from diverse authors (Node 2) into a reflective, socially situated act of literary discussion.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparative response discussion across diverse texts is genuinely rich — it builds empathy, cultural awareness, and the interpretive vocabulary students need for secondary literary study.
success_criteria: Shares a personal response to a character or event and connects it to the text's context
Explains how a reader from a different context might respond differently to the same character or event
